origin_region: Blended in Britain from Assam, Ceylon and Kenyan black teas (historically also Chinese Keemun)
processing: A blend of fully oxidised black teas, mostly broken-leaf or CTC grades, combined by a blender to a fixed house taste; nothing is added. Loose versions use larger orthodox leaf, tea bags use small CTC granules and fannings for a fast, strong brew.
harvest_season: Not a harvest: blended year-round, with the recipe adjusted each season so the cup stays the same whatever the Assam or Kenyan crop did that year.
appearance_dry: Small, dark, even broken leaf or granules; loose-leaf versions show twisted black leaf with the odd golden tip.
appearance_liquor: Deep red-brown and bright, turning tan with milk.
taste_profile: Full-bodied, malty and brisk with a firm tannic grip and a touch of toast and dried fruit; built to be drunk strong with milk and, often, sugar.

brewing.notes: Boiling water, 3–5 minutes; it is meant to be strong. Milk is the standard serve (add it after, so you can see the colour), and it is the right tea for a pot that sits on the table. Loose orthodox blends can take a short second steep.

vintage_note: The opposite of a vintage tea: the point of a breakfast blend is that this year's tin tastes like last year's, so blenders rebalance the Assam, Ceylon and Kenyan components every season and print no harvest year. Sold year-round in bags and loose, with a best-before of two to three years. What you can check is the origin list (Assam-led blends are maltier, Kenyan-led brighter and more astringent) and whether the leaf is CTC or orthodox, which decides whether it is a quick strong brew for bags or a rounder loose-leaf pot.
description:
English Breakfast is the strong, malty, milk-friendly black blend that most of the English-speaking world means by 'a cup of tea'. It is not a single tea but a recipe, typically Assam for body, Ceylon for brightness and Kenyan tea for colour and strength, and every brand has its own version; nineteenth-century blends leaned on Chinese black tea, which is why some premium versions still include a little Keemun.

The blender's job is consistency. Tea crops change with the weather, so the proportions are adjusted every season to keep the house taste exactly where customers expect it. Most of it is sold in bags made from CTC granules and fannings, which brew fast and strong, while loose-leaf versions use larger orthodox leaf and give a rounder, less aggressive cup.

In the cup it is full, malty and brisk, with enough tannin to stand up to milk and a biscuit, and it is one of the few teas that is genuinely better brewed hard: boiling water, three to five minutes, no delicacy required. Under-brewing it gives a thin, bitter cup; the common mistakes are stewing a bag for ten minutes or using water that has gone off the boil.

There is no vintage and no season to chase. Read the back of the pack for the origins, decide whether you want the quick CTC strength of a bag or the rounder loose leaf, and expect premium versions to say more about their Assam. 'Irish Breakfast' is the same idea with more Assam, 'Scottish Breakfast' stronger still.

If you want to understand what the blend is made of, drink a plain second-flush Assam and a plain Ceylon side by side; the breakfast blend is the middle of those two with Kenyan colour added.
